comment: A block written as a VALUE rather than as a bare JSX attribute: `const panel = @@( … )` outside JSX, and `css={@@( … )}` inside the braces JSX already has for an expression. The second exists because of a limit nothing here can lift — an editor stops consulting injections once it enters a tag's attribute list, so a bare block gets no colours unless it is the first attribute on the tag name's own line. The selector has TWO clauses per language and both are load-bearing: outside JSX children, and inside a braced EXPRESSION. Excluding children wholesale was written when a component had one block on its root; a block is one class per DECLARATION now, so every tag carries its own and a nested element is always inside children — measured, a nested block then had no colours at all and the rest of the file was read as type parameters and arrow functions. Asking for a braced expression keeps the one thing the exclusion was for: prose. `css=@@( … )` written in a paragraph is children TEXT and is not an expression, so it still opens nothing.
injectionSelector: L:source.tsx -meta.jsx.children -string -comment, L:source.tsx meta.embedded.expression -string -comment, L:source.ts -string -comment, L:source.js -meta.jsx.children -string -comment, L:source.js meta.embedded.expression -string -comment, L:source.js.jsx -meta.jsx.children -string -comment, L:source.js.jsx meta.embedded.expression -string -comment

value.comment: No lookbehind, and that is the point of the spelling: `@@(` is a syntax error everywhere in TypeScript — measured after `=`, on a class member, on a parameter, as a call argument and as an object value — so nothing else can be mistaken for it. `@(` needed one, because a parenthesised decorator is real TypeScript in two of those positions. The optional word between is a NAMED site — `@@keyframes(`, `@@font-face(`, `@@property(` — whose opening is not a fixed width; it is coloured as the at-rule it becomes. The `@@` is this language's MARKER and is coloured as one wherever it appears — here, on `@@if`, and on `...`. A user reported the two characters coming out as punctuation in one place and a keyword in another, which is a reader having to learn that the same marker means two things. The BRACKET keeps `punctuation.section.embedded.begin`, and that is not cosmetic: it is what pairs with the `contentName` an editor reads to treat the inside as CSS. The NAME of a named site keeps `at-rule`, which it had before: `@@` says whose language this is and `keyframes` says which at-rule, exactly as CSS scopes `@keyframes` as an at-rule keyword.
